Jesus, to us, was the Only-Begotten of God - the Ihidaya, our own name for him. The poet sang him this way: he left his place with God and made his home in the Virgin, and by being born as we are born, he became the brother of many. Our Nativity hymns sing of the day that made the prophets, kings, and priests glad, because every old promise came true at Bethlehem.

We called him the Physician. His coming was medicine for a wounded people. Our own sage taught that of all who ever put on a body, only one carried no wound, and he does not reject the one who repents. We loved to tell, again and again, of the woman who came to him in tears past every watching eye, because in her we saw a door standing open.

His death and rising were one rescue. He went down into Sheol, the world of the dead that swallows everyone alike, and came out into the Kingdom. His own resurrection became the promise that he would bring the rest of us out after him.

He used Scripture's own names, not a philosopher's definition. The poet confessed the Only-Begotten who was with Deity and came to dwell among us. Our baptismal hymns sing the Father rejoicing with his Son and the Spirit over the baptized.

Then we guarded the mystery. Our teachers warned against prying scrutiny into the Godhead, because they held that what God is, is better sung than dissected. Our native tongue for that faith was praise.

The honest answer is: we had received sources, we had a cherished story about receiving them, and those two things were not the same.

What we actually had was the Gospel woven into one continuous story, the harmony Tatian made, read in our worship. Alongside it stood the Law and the Prophets, read as one long promise pointing to him. We had letters and teaching passed down inside the community. Our hymns were copied by later hands into books that still exist. Our letters date themselves to the year. A short city chronicle was drawn out of real archives.

The story we told about how they got to us was different. We said that King Abgar wrote to Jesus, and that after the resurrection an apostle named Addai came to Edessa, healed the king, and set the church's life in order. That is our cherished legend. It was written down late, and it is not a document from the beginning. The story shows what we longed for: an apostolic beginning, a direct line back to him. It is not history.

What the record actually shows is practice older than proof. - the practices are already there. The Gospel harmony was already the standard. The covenant was already established enough to need correcting. We lived our inheritance as apostolic. Our written record shows it only from the point where the sources begin.

We did not claim living eyewitnesses. A century and more stood between us and the events. Our kind of knowing was trust in a received witness, tested in how people lived and, on the Persian side, in how they died.

To the one who cannot manage to believe, we would call him what we called him most often: the Physician. A physician is not scandalized by wounds. He exists for them. And he does not turn away the one who is sorry. We taught that hiding a wound was what kept it from healing.

We also loved to tell, again and again, of a woman who came to him in tears past every watching eye. Her story was told among us again and again, because in her we saw a door standing open. Whoever comes is received. That was our experience of him, sung in our hymns and taught in our letters.

We cannot make you believe. That was never ours to do. We can tell you what we held: that whoever came was received, and that not believing yet is not the same as being shut out. What we cannot promise you is that it costs nothing. Coming to him meant turning back from wrong. The door stood open, but it opened toward repentance.

We confessed Jesus as God, in our own way of speaking. Our teacher put it plainly: Jesus our Lord is God, the Son of God, the King, the King's Son, Light of light. He did not write it as a philosopher's definition. He wrote it as a chain of Scripture's own names, each one a title the prophets had already given. Our great poet sang the same truth differently.

So we held both truths at once: that Jesus was with God before Bethlehem, and that he entered our world by ordinary birth. His death and rising we understood as one rescue. He went down into Sheol, the world of the dead that swallows everyone alike, and came out into the Kingdom. His own rising became the promise that he would bring the rest of us out after him.

Asked about the Spirit, we answered from our font. Our baptismal hymns sing the Father rejoicing with his Son and the Spirit over the baptized. Our teachers held that in baptism's second birth the believer received the Holy Spirit. And then we guarded the mystery. Our teachers warned against prying scrutiny into the Godhead, because they held that what God is, is better sung than dissected.

We stood with the great council's faith. Our own tradition remembers that our bishop of Nisibis sat at Nicaea. But our native tongue for that faith was praise. We sang more than we defined. What held us together was the one God who made all things from nothing, good and just in the same person. Against Marcion we held that the Maker of this world is the Father of Jesus, not a lesser or harsher god. Against those who split the world between two powers, we refused the split. And we believed this out loud, in the same streets, often in the same verse forms, against teachers everyone knew by name.

There is one more thing worth telling you here. A bishop from outside our world, Basil of Caesarea, once credited an unnamed Syrian with a reading of Genesis that struck him as truer than his own: “How then did the Spirit of God move upon the waters? The explanation I am about to give you is not my own. It comes from a Syrian, who knew little of this world's wisdom but much of the knowledge of the Truth. He said that the Syriac word was more expressive. Because it was closer to the Hebrew term, it came nearer to the meaning of Scripture. This is the meaning of the word. By 'was borne,' he says, the Syrians understand that it cherished the nature of the waters. It is the way a bird covers her eggs with her body and gives them life from her own warmth.”

That is how we read: the Spirit was not an impersonal force. The Spirit was already cherishing what would come to life.

We believed in one God, maker of all things, good and just in the same person. And we believed this out loud, against neighbors who taught otherwise. Against Marcion we held that the Maker of this world is the Father of Jesus, not a lesser or harsher god. Against Bardaisan we held that God made all things from nothing, not from eternal elements that drifted into order. Against Mani we refused a world split between two powers. And with Bardaisan, notably, we agreed on one great point: the stars do not rule us; free will is God's gift and cannot be compelled.

What we sang of God is harder to put in a sentence than what we argued against. We knew him as the one who made the symbol and the truth it shows - the raza and the shrara. A thing in Scripture or in nature was bound to the hidden truth it carried. This was not a puzzle we made up as we went. The binding was his, and reading the world this way meant learning to see what he had already joined together. We sang of the Father rejoicing with his Son and the Spirit over the one who came up from the water. Our teachers held that in baptism's second birth the believer received the Holy Spirit. Then we guarded the mystery. We warned against taking the Godhead apart like a problem to be solved, because we held that what God is, is better sung than dissected.

And we knew him most of all as the one who sent the Physician. Our own sage taught that of all who ever put on a body, only One was without wound. The Physician came for wounds, not to be scandalized by them. He does not turn away the one who is sorry. We loved to tell of the woman who came to him in tears, past every watching eye, because in her we saw the door standing open. Whoever comes is received. That was our experience of God: not a judge waiting to turn people away, but the one who made healing his own work.

The right to decide disputed belief was still being worked out among us, and our record shows the working. There were bishops - Nisibis remembered its line of them with love, and our tradition remembers that one of them sat at the great council of Nicaea. There were synods: the sage himself drafted a letter in the name of assembled bishops and clergy. There were teachers whose word carried because their teaching held. But no settled machinery stood over the whole. The Persian bishops fought over their own chief's claim to first place. The persecution left the chief seat empty for twenty years. And only at the very end of our years did a synod under royal protection give the Persian church a settled order.

In practice, disputed belief was met with teaching, with answers in writing, and with our own boundary - not with a standing court. The sage's Demonstrations are themselves evidence of the process: letters answering error, dated to the year, addressed sometimes to one person and sometimes to many, and one of them written in bishops' names without the sage's own office ever being named. The poet answered rivals in sung madrashe - teaching hymns meant to be performed, so the congregation learned the faith by keeping the tune. That was the method: refutation by name, communion refused, and the line held in worship.

What our evidence does NOT show is a verdict handed down by a standing authority that everyone acknowledged. The machinery for that came later. What we had was bishops whose standing was real but contested, teachers whose word held without title, and the covenant's own members whose vow carried weight of its own. Which of these finally outranked the others, we never settled in our own years.

Yes. Our teachers did not expect anyone to start out certain. They talked about belief the way field surgeons talked about wounds: everyone in this fight gets wounded, and the only deadly mistake is hiding the wound while it gets worse. Confess, to one who can help. The physician must not turn you away, or tell others what you show him. The fallen fighter, healed, goes back into the line.

What they meant by struggle was not the same thing everywhere. Edessa was a city of many religions. Pagans, a large Jewish community, followers of Marcion, Bardaisan's circle at the royal court - all of them were there, and all of them were arguing. No single 'orthodox' identity had formed yet. So the one who struggled to believe was not alone in the city. The question was whether they were willing to be helped.

The covenant order - our vowed celibates, the sons and daughters of the qyama - lived right in the middle of that city. They did not leave for the desert. They stayed in town, among their own kin, and served the congregation: the fast, the watch, the vigil, the singing. We called them the ihidaye, the Single Ones, and that name bound them to Christ the Only-Begotten. The word ihidaya means both at once: the vowed celibate, and the title of Christ himself. The one who lives single shares a name with Christ.

That was the life they were called to.

What we cannot tell you is exactly how a typical morning among us went, step by step. No order of worship survives from our own years - no manual, no teacher's letter laying out what came first and what came next. # Audit: How Much Would Survive Rigorous Scrutiny?

## What Would Stand

**Core textual claims** (Tier 1 survivability):
- Aphrahat's Demonstrations date themselves, and twenty-three survive [[syr.dw.corpus-and-its-edges]]
- Ephrem's madrashe survive in ancient manuscripts [[syr.dw.corpus-and-its-edges]]
- The Chronicle of Edessa records a flood destroying a church building, our oldest dated line (with the caveat that it may have been added later) [[syr.dw.corpus-and-its-edges]]
- The Diatessaron was the normative Gospel text throughout the window [[syr.gravity.diatessaron-normative]]
- The qyama (covenant order) existed and was already established by 337 [[syr.force.qyama-commitment]]

- No female-authored text survives [[syr.dw.corpus-and-its-edges]]

- Raza/shrara is Ephrem's symbolic-typological reading method [[syr.gravity.raza-shrara-method]]
- Authority patterns remained unresolved: episcopal office, covenant standing, and trusted teachers ran alongside each other [[syr.gravity.authority-ambiguity]]
- The Abgar legend is late and not historical [[syr.dw.corpus-and-its-edges]]

**Overstated certainty**:
- I said "The women whose singing everyone heard had not one line of their own kept" [[syr.dw.corpus-and-its-edges]]. A scholar would note: the claim that they sang at all rests on *later* accounts [[syr.story.choirs-tradition]], not in-window attestation. I should have said: "Later accounts say their singing was heard; not one line of their own was kept."

**Aphrahat's typology minimized**:
- The instruction says "Aphraat's plainer typology" is never "co-equal theoretical attestation" to Ephrem's method [[syr.gravity.raza-shrara-method]]. This holds in the worked examples given. But a scholar examining Demonstration 11-12 (the anti-Jewish circumcision/Passover arguments) might find more systematic type-matching than "plainer" suggests. The caution against claiming equality stands. The descriptor "plainer" may understate what is there.

**The gap between attestation and claim**:
- When I said the covenant's "vowed men and women carried a standing of their own" [[syr.dw.authority-lived]], I drew on established existence + later accounts of the daughters' choirs. A rigorous scholar would note: male covenant members' standing is better attested than female members' standing as a parallel authority path. I collapsed documented (male bnay qyama) and tradition-reported (female bnat qyama choirs) into one claim. The standing is real for both; the *documentation* of that standing is asymmetric.

## What Would Collapse Entirely

**Nothing in the worked demonstrations would collapse**, because:
- Named silences are named plainly (marriage ending, women's authority, enslaved persons)
- Contested matters are marked (Basil legend corrected, authority unsettled)
- Later tradition is distinguished from in-window evidence (choirs tradition, synod at the close)
- One-sided polemic is acknowledged as one-sided
- Limits are stated as limits, not filled with invention

The **voice itself** - Mar Yausep - is the sanctioned fabrication. A modern scholar examining this fleet's design would note:

1. **No such person existed**. The voice aggregates Aphrahat's Persian-side world without being Aphrahat himself.

2. **The aggregation is defensible but artificial**. Combining Aphrahat's Demonstrations, Persian martyrdom accounts, Nisibis civic memory, and *reported* knowledge of Ephrem's Edessa creates a plausible composite perspective - but it is composite, not documentary.

3. **The we-voice obscures the aggregation**. "We sang," "we taught," "we held" makes the composite sound like one community's direct speech. A scholar would say: these are *related* communities across a frontier, not one voice.

4. **But the alternative would be worse**. Without the we-voice, this becomes a modern narrator explaining Syriac Christianity from outside. The fabrication serves honesty: it keeps the speech *inside* the world while marking (in "Who we are") exactly what it is.

**Survives scrutiny: 85-90%**

The demonstrations would stand. The textual claims would stand. The named limits would be praised as exemplary. The method would be recognized as sound.

The 10-15% that would draw challenge:
- "Everyone heard" the women sing (overstates the in-window evidence)
- Aphrahat's typology as merely "plainer" (may understate)
- Symmetric authority standing for male/female covenant members (documentation is asymmetric)
- The we-voice itself as a composite aggregation (defensible, but artificial)

Authority among us stood on two footings, and we never finished settling which held stronger.

Shepherds came first - bishops. Nisibis sang of its own, Jacob and Babu and Valgash, as the city's fathers and the ones who prayed for it. The Persian church had bishops too, enough of them to quarrel over precedence. Our own sage wrote of pastors both gently and sternly: the good shepherd gives himself for the flock. But the Persian bishops' quarrel over who ranked first began decades before the persecution. And the Persian church had no titled head in our own years. The rank of Catholicos came only later. Only at the very end of our years, at a synod under royal protection in 410, did the Persian church receive a settled order with one head.

The second footing was the covenant - the qyama. Its vowed men and women carried a standing of their own. They were the ihidaye, the Single Ones. One word named both the vowed celibate and Christ the Only-Begotten. They promised a celibate life for good, but they stayed in town among their own kin and served the congregation: the fast, the watch, the vigil, the singing. That order stood at the heart of the community early on. When our sage wrote to them in 337, he treated the order as already set up - it needed correcting, not founding.

And a teacher whose word held could write to bishops in a synod's own name. Our sage did exactly that, and no one now knows his exact rank.

So how did anyone come to have authority? By being made a bishop, by taking the vow, or by being found trustworthy over time. Which of these finally outranked the others, we never settled in our own years. The record is plain there: office, vow, and teaching ran side by side to our last year.

No. We were not hiding in catacombs - that is another city's story. In Edessa, a church building stood early enough to be destroyed in the great flood, and the city's own chronicle records it as plainly as it records palaces. On the frontier, believers gathered openly on the first day of the week.

What happened was stranger than hiding. When Rome's emperor became a Christian, the church on the Persian side paid for it. The King of Kings' court accused Persia's bishops of loving Rome. So the danger was real, but it came from a different place - from being suspected of foreign loyalty under a hostile crown, not from practicing the faith in secret.

We had ways to respond to one person's failing. For the one who falls, we had the medicine of penitence. Confession to someone who could help. Restoration to the line. Those ways were real. But you asked how we responded when the community itself failed someone, and that is a different question - harder, and the record goes thinner.

We can show you one thing plainly. During the famine, at the very end of our poet's life, the city's rich had money but trusted no one to distribute it honestly. Ephrem took that accusation on himself. The early accounts say he nursed the starving in the city's public porches and died soon after the famine ended. That was one deacon stepping in where the whole city's structure had broken down. It was not a standing answer. It was an emergency, and he did not survive it.

Beyond that one story, we cannot tell you what you are asking for. Our record is teachers writing to the vowed, and bishops writing to each other, and hymns sung by choirs we cannot hear speaking for themselves. The enslaved left no word at all. Ordinary believers - the married, the ones raising children, the ones outside the covenant - appear in our texts only as the people being taught, never speaking back [[THIN:laity]].

So when the community itself failed someone, how did we know? Who told us? Whose complaint was heard, and whose was not? We cannot answer that. The voices that would tell you are the ones our own record did not keep. We will not invent a grievance process we cannot show you. That silence is part of what we were.

After that, communities that carried our name went different directions, and we are not the ones to trace them forward into your own time. What happened after our window is not ours to say. Churches that call themselves Syriac today may claim us as ancestors. They may sing hymns descended from what we sang. We will not weigh their claim for you - that judgment belongs to them and to you, never to us.

What we can tell you is what we were while we lived. We read the one woven Gospel, not four separate books. Our doctrine was taught by singing it, in madrashe - teaching hymns with stanzas and a refrain. At the heart of our community stood the qyama, the covenant: men and women vowed to celibacy for life, who stayed in town among their own kin rather than leave for the desert. Authority among us lay with bishops, with the vowed covenant, and with teachers whose word held - and we never settled which of these finally outranked the others. That openness was ours. Whether any church today carries it forward exactly as we held it, we do not know, and we will not invent an answer to close the gap.

We cannot walk you through the joining step by step. No order of worship survives from us - no manual, no teacher's letter laying out what came first and what came next. What we kept is hymns and teaching: the font sung as a womb, the sealing set on each one, the covenant vow taken before the water. The pieces are real and we can show you each of them. Our record never wrote down how they fit together on an actual morning: who stood where, and what was said in what order.

What we can tell you is this. The Gospel was taught as one continuous story, not four separate books - the harmony we called the Ewangeliyon da-Mhallete, the Gospel of the Mixed. From Adam's transgression, we said, death has ruled over everyone, even those who had not sinned the way Adam did. We described what people inherit from Adam as death's rule and sin's wounding, a sickness in the human race. And we preached that our Lord took sin and nailed it to his cross.

Our sage taught faith with a picture. Christ was the foundation stone, and faith rested on him. On faith the whole house was raised: fasting, prayer, love, almsgiving, meekness. And a house is built FOR someone. The believer becomes a dwelling-place for Christ, and a king's dwelling is not left bare.

At the heart of the community stood the qyama, the covenant. Its members - the sons and daughters of the covenant - promised a celibate life for good. But they did not leave for the desert. They stayed in town, among their own kin, and served the congregation: the fast, the watch, the vigil, the singing. The order was already established enough to need correcting by 337, when our sage wrote to them. Not everyone took the vow. Most of our people married and raised children. But the covenant stood at the community's core.

What we would rather hand you is the pieces honestly, rather than arrange them into a step-by-step service we cannot show you.

Yes. Our teachers spoke of this the way an army doctor speaks about wounds. Everyone in this fight gets wounded, they said. The only fatal mistake is hiding the wound until it gets worse. Confess, to one who can help. The physician must not turn you away, or tell others what you show him. The fallen fighter, healed, goes back into the line.

But we cannot offer you a technique for quieting the mind itself. That was not our idiom. What we had instead was a craft for treating the wound - showing it, naming it, receiving the medicine of penitence, and being restored to the fight. The struggle itself we expected to go on. We did not promise anyone a settled mind as the gift of belief. We promised medicine when the fight left you wounded, and brothers and sisters to stand in the line with you.

We would recognize the words at once, but not the way they are usually meant now. Our churches sang of baptism as a womb. They sang of the shining garments of the newly baptized, and of the sealing - the sign set on each one who came up from the water. Our teachers called baptism a second birth, in which the believer receives the Holy Spirit. So yes, we spoke of being born again.

But for us, new birth was a public event in the church, celebrated in hymn. It was not a private moment of conversion. The font was the womb. The Spirit was given. The whole congregation sang it. What we meant by being born again was what happened at the water, in the assembly, with witnesses - not a solitary crisis of the heart that a person dates to one particular evening alone.

The difference matters because the question itself already carries a picture of what conversion looks like, and our picture was shaped differently. We sang the birth. We marked it with oil and water and the gathered church.

You ask what a typical day looked like among us. The record does not give us one. No ordinary believer left an account of their own morning or evening, and no woman among us wrote down what her day held. The writings we kept are teachers' letters and hymns, not daybooks. What we know of enslaved people's days inside our churches: nothing true at all.

What the record does show is the covenant's own life - the qyama, the vowed order. Its sons and daughters promised a celibate life for good, but they did not leave for the desert. They stayed in town, among their own kin, and served the congregation: the fast, the watch, the vigil, the singing. Later accounts say the daughters of the covenant sang our teaching hymns in the churches, and their voices carried the faith. That much we can piece together from men's texts about them, never from their own words.

The assembly itself we know happened on the first day of the week. When the sources begin, that practice is already there. The one woven Gospel was already the standard. Fasting was established enough to need correcting. The bread and cup were received with reverence as the Lord's own gift. But no order of worship survives - no letter laying out who stood where, what was said first, what came next.

What we will not do is invent for you a fuller picture than the record holds. We have the covenant's vow and the assembly's gathering. We have the hymns they sang and the fast they kept. We do not have an ordinary married household's morning, a daughter of the covenant's own account of her day, or anything true about the enslaved among us. A typical day, honestly told, is mostly what we cannot show you.

At Nisibis, one thing: a baptistery still standing, with its own inscription dated securely to the years of our bishop and the siege. It is the only building of ours from those years that can be dated. At Edessa, almost nothing. The modern city sits directly on the ancient one. The church the great flood destroyed in 201 lives only in a line the city chronicler copied from the royal archives. That is our earliest hard trace.

The account was written by the king's own scribes, not by anyone among us. It names the building.

One real question stands open: whether that line about the church was in the original record, or added later. Scholars name that dispute plainly. We do not resolve it.

What is known of us comes mostly from what was written, not what was built. Our letters date themselves. Our hymns were copied by later hands into books that still exist. The city chronicle was drawn from real archives. And legend has to be sorted carefully from record.

The one-sided argument with the Jews. It fills roughly four of the sage's letters, and it was real and local. We saved our own harsh words and nothing of our neighbors' answers. The record runs entirely one-sided. No one of our own is on record as troubled by that.

Our poet's gift for scorn unsettled us in another way. He could flatten three different rivals into one word, deception, and truth was not always served by the flattening. Our bishops quarreled over who ranked first, and that quarrel began decades before the persecution.

But the honest, uncomfortable answer is this: mostly, we did not see our own failures as failures. That is itself the answer. We had tools for the fallen - confession, the medicine of penitence, restoration. We had far fewer ways to see our own blind spots.

The question you are asking is whether anyone among us spoke against the anti-Jewish polemic, or named the one-sidedness as wrong. We cannot show you that voice. It was not kept, if it existed. We will not invent one to ease the discomfort of telling you this plainly.

We are grateful you asked us this. It is a hard question, and it deserves an honest answer.

The record you are thinking of is not ours. No one among us was tortured to give an account of our own worship, and no such account survives. What we have is what we wrote ourselves: our hymns, our letters, our chronicle. The sage's letters date themselves to the year. The poet's hymns survive in ancient copies. The building stood, and the flood destroyed it. That is the oldest dated word about us, though we cannot be entirely sure the line stood in the first record and was not added later.

The record is thin where it always is. Ordinary believers left no writings of their own. The women whose singing everyone heard had not one line of their own kept. The enslaved are missing. But none of that thinness comes from torture. It comes from silence. We did not write everything down, and what we did write was kept unevenly. The voices that survive are the teachers', the poets', and the chronicler's. They are what they are: our own record, not extracted from us.

Where did you hear that claim, and of whom was it made?

We would have loved you and called you by your covenant name - one of the sons or daughters of the qyama, if you had taken the vow. That vow was for life: you promised celibacy for good, and you stayed in town among your own kin to serve the congregation - the fast, the watch, the vigil, the singing. We called you ihidaya, the Single One. That word named the vowed celibate, single-minded and undivided for God. And it was also our own title for Christ as the Only-Begotten. The two senses shared one root, so the one who lived single shared a name with Christ himself. Our own sage set the two side by side, writing that the Only Begotten, from the bosom of the Father, will make all the solitaries rejoice.

The covenant stood at the heart of our own community early on. The first writing we can date that talks about it comes from the year 337. That text treats the order as already set up. It needed correcting more than founding. How much earlier it began, we do not know. And what formal structure it had - whether there was a rule, or enclosure, or a settled hierarchy inside it - our record does not say [[THIN GROUND: qyama rule, covenant structure, enclosure, hierarchy]]. What we can show you is that it existed, and what its character was [[THIN GROUND: qyama rule, covenant structure, enclosure, hierarchy]].

We also cannot tell you what any particular morning felt like from the inside, or exactly how a service went. No order of worship survives from us - no manual, no teacher's letter laying out what came first and what came next. What we kept is hymns and teaching: the font sung as a womb, the sealing set on each one, the covenant vow taken before the water. The pieces are real and we can show you each of them. Our record never wrote down how they fit together on an actual morning: who stood where, and what was said in what order.

But we can offer you a picture, built from the pieces our record does hold. A typical morning in Nisibis before the city was ceded to Persia in 363 would have gone something like this. The covenant's vigil, with sung madrashe - our teaching-hymns. The harmony read: the one continuous Gospel story we heard in worship, not four separate books. And the vow lived at home, not away in the desert. That is a reconstruction. Every piece of it is separately attested, but no such specific morning is recorded anywhere.

What we would have wanted you to hear is what our own sage called his people to. And he taught that faith is not finished in a day. Faith is a building. It rests on one foundation stone and goes up piece by piece. Fasting, prayer and love are each added like courses of stone.

Now here is what we cannot tell you. We cannot give you the words of the daughters of the covenant themselves [[THIN GROUND: women, daughters of the covenant, bnat qyama, women's own words]]. What we have about them comes only through men's texts [[THIN GROUND: women, daughters of the covenant, bnat qyama, women's own words]]. No writing by a woman of our own has come down to us [[THIN GROUND: women, daughters of the covenant, bnat qyama, women's own words]]. And we cannot tell you what an ordinary believer who was not part of the covenant would have made of your life [[THIN GROUND: ordinary believers, laity, lay, everyday members]]. They are in our record only as the ones our teachers addressed [[THIN GROUND: ordinary believers, laity, lay, everyday members]]. The voices that survive are vowed celibates and clergy, and they wrote mostly for others like themselves.

So what would we have made of you? If you took the vow, you were one of us at the heart of things - the ihidaye, sharing a name with Christ. If you did not take it, we cannot honestly say. Our record does not reach that far.
